summary:
Canary is a browser-based health monitor that helps astronauts assess their own health on long missions, when Earth is too far away for real-time help. On a Mars transit, signals can take up to about 20 minutes each way, so the astronaut is the first responder.

Instead of judging readings against a population “normal,” Canary learns each astronaut’s personal baseline from their first seven days. It then uses a statistical drift detector (CUSUM) to catch small, sustained changes in sleep, reaction time, mood, heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, and temperature. Indicators are combined by body region to reduce false alarms, and hard safety limits always override the baseline. A clickable body figure, trend charts, plain-language guidance, a radiation dose tracker, and a one-click flight surgeon summary help the crew act. Advice changes for a space station, lunar base, or Mars transit, and the app works offline.

Canary is a prototype built around NASA’s five spaceflight hazards. It runs on simulated data, and its thresholds are illustrative, not clinical. It’s designed to give crews an early warning before a problem becomes a crisis.
details:
What it does and how it works

Canary is a self-assessment tool for astronauts on long missions, built for the situation where Earth is too far away for real-time medical help. The crew logs daily readings: sleep, reaction time, attention lapses, mood, heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, and temperature.

For each astronaut, Canary learns a personal baseline from the first seven days of the mission, using the median and the median absolute deviation, which resist outliers. It then runs a two-sided CUSUM drift detector on every indicator to catch small, sustained changes that a single reading would miss. A body region only flags when enough of its related indicators drift together, which cuts down on false alarms. Hard safety limits, such as a high fever or dangerous blood pressure, always override the baseline.

The astronaut sees all of this through a clickable body figure that shows each region’s status by color and label. Trend charts show the astronaut’s own normal range, with sustained drift marked. Plain-language panels explain how to take each measurement and what to do next. Canary also includes a radiation dose tracker with a solar-event warning, a five-tap reaction check that feeds into the log, and a one-click summary for the flight surgeon. Its advice changes by environment: space station, lunar base, or Mars transit.

Benefits

Canary gives astronauts an early warning, not just a reading. A standard vitals check asks whether a number falls inside a population range. Canary asks whether this person has moved away from their own normal. That matters in a small crew, where individual differences are large and a value that is fine for one astronaut can be a warning for another. By tracking sleep, reaction time, attention lapses, and mood alongside heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, and temperature, it can show a drift in the overall pattern while each vital sign is still within its usual range.

The astronaut also gets help acting on it. Every alert says what changed, how long the drift has lasted, and how confident the tool is. It lists the likely contributors, such as less sleep and slower reactions, and recommends a next step. Each indicator has a short note on how to measure it, so crew members don’t need medical training to use the tool. The safety limits stay in place, so a personal baseline can never hide a dangerous value.

For the mission as a whole, Canary works offline, so nothing depends on a connection to Earth. That matters when messages can take 20 minutes or more each way. When a consult is needed, the one-click summary gives the flight surgeon a clear picture of the trends, safety limits, radiation total, and suggested actions, so the surgeon can spend time on the problem instead of collecting basic information.

Intended impact

The intended impact is to give crews on long-duration missions more autonomy in managing their own health. As missions move toward the Moon and Mars, astronauts will spend longer periods far from real-time medical support. Canary is meant to be one tool that helps them notice problems earlier, understand what is changing, and decide whether to manage it themselves, ask a crewmate, or consult the ground. Over the long term, we hope earlier detection can reduce the chance that a small, manageable change becomes a serious problem far from help.

I also see a possible impact on how remote medical teams work. Because Canary produces a structured summary of an astronaut’s trends, consultations across a communication delay could be better prepared and more efficient, with a single message carrying what might otherwise take several back-and-forth exchanges.

The same approach could be useful beyond spaceflight. Many people work in isolated, confined, or hard-to-reach settings, such as polar stations, submarines, remote research camps, and offshore platforms. Self-baselined monitoring with transparent explanations could help them as well. We want to be clear that Canary is a prototype running on simulated data with illustrative thresholds. It is decision support, not a diagnosis, and it would need validation on real data and review by clinicians and flight surgeons before any real use.

Tools and technologies

I built Canary with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using SVG for the body figure and charts. There are no frameworks, no server, and no database, so everything runs in the browser. The app is hosted on Vercel, the code is on GitHub, and the slides were made in Canva. No special hardware is required.

The app runs on simulated mission data that we generate in the code. We did not use NASA datasets directly. Instead, we built on NASA’s Human Research Program framework of five spaceflight hazards and on the Mars communication-delay constraint. We used Claude, an AI assistant, to help debug the code.

Creativity

The central idea is to compare each astronaut to themselves, not to a population average. The name comes from the “canary in the coal mine,” a living early-warning signal that showed trouble before people could feel it. I applied that idea to health: instead of waiting for a vital sign to cross a threshold, Canary watches for the small, sustained shifts that appear first.

Several design choices follow from that idea. Combining indicators by body region means a region only flags when several related measures drift together, which makes alerts more meaningful and less noisy. The safety limits override the baseline, so the personalized approach never becomes a safety risk. The escalation advice depends on distance from Earth, so the same drift produces different guidance on a space station, a lunar base, and a Mars transit. That ties the tool directly to the constraint the challenge highlights: astronauts must assess themselves when help is far away.

I also tried to make the experience clear for people who aren’t medical experts. The clickable body figure shows status by color and by text. Each region explains its function and the hazards that affect it, and every alert is written in plain language with a confidence label. The radiation tracker covers a hazard that daily vitals can’t detect, and the reaction check brings a simple cognitive measure into the same workflow. All of it runs in a single web page with no server, which keeps it simple, fast, and usable offline.

Factors we considered

False alarms: combining indicators by region and requiring sustained drift before flagging.

Safety: absolute limits that a personal baseline can never hide.

Honesty: confidence labels, and a clear statement that this is a prototype on simulated data with illustrative thresholds.

Autonomy: offline operation and advice that depends on distance from Earth.

Clarity: color-coded status with text labels, controls that can be used with a keyboard, and explanations written for non-experts.

Known limits: repeated cognitive tests have practice effects, so real use would need several baseline sessions, and the drift engine still needs validation on real sleep and reaction-time data.
